question: A development team runs each microservice on its own EC2 instance with a full guest operating system. Instances take minutes to boot, and most of them are lightly used. The team wants faster startup and higher density on the same hardware. Why would moving the services to containers help?
options: Containers include their own hypervisor, so each container runs a separate kernel with dedicated hardware
Containers run only on serverless platforms, so the team would no longer pay for any compute capacity
Containers share the host operating system kernel, so they are lighter than virtual machines and start in seconds
Containers store application state permanently in the image, so no external database is needed
explanation: Containers package an application and its dependencies but share the host kernel, so they avoid booting a full operating system and many can run on one host. Containers do not include a hypervisor or a separate kernel. They run on EC2, Fargate, on premises, and elsewhere, and compute is still billed. Container file systems are temporary, so persistent state still belongs in external storage.

question: A CI pipeline pushes a new image to an Amazon ECR repository on every commit, and storage costs keep growing. The team needs to keep only the 20 most recent tagged release images and remove untagged images after 7 days. Which solution meets this requirement with the LEAST operational overhead?
options: Write a scheduled AWS Lambda function that lists images through the ECR API every night and deletes everything except the latest 20 releases
Enable ECR cross-Region replication so that older images are moved to a Region with lower storage prices
Create an ECR lifecycle policy with rules that expire untagged images older than 7 days and keep only the last 20 tagged images
Turn on tag immutability so that each new push replaces the stored layers of the previous image with the same tag
explanation: ECR lifecycle policies automatically expire images by age or count and by tag status, with no code to maintain. A scheduled Lambda function works but adds code and operations. Replication copies images to another Region, which increases storage. Tag immutability prevents tags from being overwritten; it does not remove old images.

question: A security team wants every container image in Amazon ECR to be checked for vulnerabilities in both operating system packages and application language packages, rechecked automatically when new CVEs are published, and wants critical findings to alert the team right away. Which actions meet these requirements? (Select TWO.)
options: Enable ECR basic scanning with scan on push so that every image is checked when it is pushed to the repository
Create an Amazon EventBridge rule that matches critical Inspector findings and sends them to an Amazon SNS topic
Enable Amazon GuardDuty Runtime Monitoring for the clusters that run the images to detect vulnerable packages
Enable ECR enhanced scanning with Amazon Inspector in continuous scanning mode
Enable AWS Config rules that compare running image digests with an approved list maintained by the security team
explanation: Enhanced scanning uses Amazon Inspector to scan operating system and programming language packages and rescans images continuously as new vulnerabilities are published. Inspector findings are sent to EventBridge, where a rule can notify the team through SNS. Basic scanning runs on push or manually and covers fewer package types. GuardDuty and AWS Config do not perform CVE scanning of ECR images.

question: A company deploys containerized services from Amazon ECR in us-east-1 and has a disaster recovery environment in eu-west-1. If us-east-1 is unavailable, the DR environment must be able to pull the latest images from inside its own Region. Which solution meets this requirement with the LEAST operational overhead?
options: Configure the DR tasks to keep pulling images from the us-east-1 repository URI, which ECS can reach from any Region
Configure ECR registry replication rules that copy the repositories from us-east-1 to eu-west-1
Export the images to an S3 bucket nightly with a script and use S3 Cross-Region Replication to copy them to eu-west-1
Rebuild every image in eu-west-1 from source code with AWS CodeBuild when a disaster is declared
explanation: ECR replication automatically copies images pushed to the source registry into the destination Region, so the DR environment can pull locally even if the primary Region fails. Pulling from us-east-1 fails exactly when DR is needed. Exporting to S3 and reimporting adds custom steps. Rebuilding during a disaster slows recovery and may produce different images.

question: A company stores its container images in an Amazon ECR repository in a central shared-services account. Amazon ECS tasks in a separate production account must pull these images. Which actions should a solutions architect take? (Select TWO.)
options: Make the repository public so that any account can pull images without credentials
Create an IAM user in the shared-services account and store its keys in the task definition
Add a repository policy in the shared-services account that allows the production account to pull images
Grant the ECS task execution role in the production account permission to call the ECR pull actions
Grant the ECS task role in the production account permission to call s3:GetObject on the repository
explanation: Cross-account access needs both sides: the repository policy in the central account allows the production account, and the execution role that pulls the image needs ECR permissions in its own account. A public repository exposes private images. Storing IAM user keys in task definitions is insecure. The task role is used by the application code, and ECR pulls are not done through S3 permissions.

question: An auditor found that a developer pushed a new image with the existing tag 'v2.3.1', which silently changed what production deployed. The company wants to make sure a released tag always refers to the same image. What should a solutions architect do?
options: Enable tag immutability on the Amazon ECR repository
Enable ECR enhanced scanning on the repository
Create a lifecycle policy that expires images older than 30 days
Enable encryption with a customer managed AWS KMS key on the repository
explanation: With tag immutability, ECR rejects any push that tries to reuse an existing tag, so a release tag can never point to a different image. Enhanced scanning finds vulnerabilities but does not protect tags. Lifecycle policies delete images. KMS encryption protects images at rest but does not stop tags from being overwritten.

question: Builds and Amazon EKS nodes in a company's VPCs pull public base images from Docker Hub. Deployments sometimes fail because of Docker Hub rate limits and outages. The company wants to keep using the same upstream images with minimal changes and with images stored inside AWS. Which solution meets these requirements?
options: Create an Amazon ECR pull-through cache rule for Docker Hub and change image references to the ECR cache repository
Configure ECR replication rules that copy images from Docker Hub into the company's private registry on a schedule
Add more NAT gateways in each VPC so that image pulls come from more source IP addresses and stay under the rate limits
Enable ECR enhanced scanning so that Docker Hub images are scanned and stored in ECR before they are pulled
explanation: A pull-through cache rule makes ECR fetch an upstream image the first time it is requested and serve cached copies after that, which avoids repeated Docker Hub pulls and their rate limits. ECR replication works only between ECR registries. Adding NAT gateways to get around rate limits is costly and unreliable. Scanning does not change where images are pulled from.

question: A containerized application running as Amazon ECS tasks on AWS Fargate must write items to an Amazon DynamoDB table. The security team prohibits long-term credentials in containers. How should the application get permissions?
options: Add the DynamoDB permissions to the task execution role, which ECS already uses to provide credentials to the task
Store an IAM user's access keys as encrypted environment variables in the task definition
Attach an IAM instance profile with DynamoDB permissions to the Fargate tasks through the capacity provider
Create an IAM role with the DynamoDB permissions and specify it as the task role in the task definition
explanation: The task role supplies temporary credentials to the application code inside the containers, which is the right place for DynamoDB permissions. The execution role is used by the ECS agent for pulling images, sending logs, and fetching secrets, not by the application. Long-term keys break the security rule. Fargate has no instances, so instance profiles do not apply.

question: An Amazon ECS task definition for a Fargate service pulls its image from a private Amazon ECR repository, uses the awslogs log driver, and injects a database password from AWS Secrets Manager as an environment variable. Which actions are performed with the task execution role? (Select THREE.)
options: Writing application data to an Amazon S3 bucket from the application code
Sending the container logs to Amazon CloudWatch Logs through the awslogs driver
Pulling the container image from the private ECR repository
Registering EC2 container instances with the ECS cluster
Answering health checks sent by the Application Load Balancer
Retrieving the Secrets Manager secret referenced in the task definition
explanation: The execution role is used by ECS and Fargate to pull images, send logs with the awslogs driver, and fetch secrets referenced in the task definition before the container starts. Calls made by the application code, such as writing to S3, use the task role. Registering container instances uses the EC2 instance role on the EC2 launch type. Load balancer health checks are network traffic and need no IAM role.

question: A company runs a web API as Amazon ECS tasks. When a task crashes, it is not replaced until an engineer starts a new one by hand. Which ECS feature should be used so that a set number of tasks always keeps running?
options: A standalone task started with the RunTask API
A task definition revision with higher CPU and memory
An ECS service with a desired count of tasks
A scheduled task triggered by Amazon EventBridge
explanation: An ECS service keeps the desired number of tasks running and replaces tasks that stop or fail health checks, and it can register them with a load balancer. Standalone tasks are not replaced when they stop. A task definition is only a blueprint and does not keep tasks running. Scheduled tasks run on a timetable and do not watch over long-running tasks.

question: A company runs several copies of the same container on each EC2 container instance in an Amazon ECS cluster that uses the EC2 launch type and bridge network mode. Each container listens on port 8080. The company needs an Application Load Balancer to spread traffic across all copies. How should the task definition be configured?
options: Set the host port to 8080 for every task so that the target group can health check every copy on a single port
Set the host port to 0 so that ECS uses dynamic host port mapping and registers each task's port with the target group
Use host network mode so that all containers share port 8080 on the instance's network interface for the best performance
Place each container copy in a separate ECS cluster so that the host ports on an instance never conflict
explanation: With dynamic port mapping, each container gets a random host port, and ECS registers each instance and port pair with the ALB target group, so many copies can run on one instance. A fixed host port of 8080 allows only one copy per instance. Host network mode has the same port conflict. Separate clusters add management work and do not solve the mapping problem.

question: A startup wants to run containerized microservices on Amazon ECS without provisioning, patching, or scaling any EC2 instances. Which option meets this requirement?
options: Use the EC2 launch type with an Auto Scaling group
Use ECS Anywhere with external instances
Use the AWS Fargate launch type for the ECS tasks
Use the EC2 launch type with Spot Instances
explanation: Fargate runs each task on capacity managed by AWS, so there are no instances to provision, patch, or scale. The EC2 launch type, with or without Spot Instances, still requires managing the instances. ECS Anywhere runs tasks on servers that the customer manages.

question: A company runs nightly image-thumbnail jobs as Amazon ECS tasks on AWS Fargate. The jobs are stateless, can be retried, and may finish at any time before morning. The company wants to reduce compute costs as much as possible without managing servers. Which option should a solutions architect recommend?
options: Run the tasks on Fargate with a Compute Savings Plan sized for peak usage
Run the tasks on EC2 On-Demand Instances in a dedicated cluster
Run the tasks on Fargate with more vCPU so they finish sooner
Run the tasks on Fargate Spot capacity
explanation: Fargate Spot runs tasks on spare capacity at a large discount, and interruptions, which come with a two-minute warning, are acceptable for retryable stateless jobs. A Savings Plan needs a steady commitment and gives a smaller discount for this part-time workload. EC2 On-Demand Instances add server management and cost more. More vCPU raises the price per second without guaranteed savings.

question: An ECS service on AWS Fargate must always have at least 4 tasks on regular Fargate capacity to stay available. Any additional tasks during busy periods should be split so that about three of every four extra tasks run on Fargate Spot to save money. How should the capacity provider strategy be configured?
options: FARGATE with weight 4, and FARGATE_SPOT with base 3 and weight 1
FARGATE_SPOT with base 4 and weight 3, and FARGATE with weight 1
FARGATE with base 4 and weight 1, and FARGATE_SPOT with weight 3
FARGATE with base 1 and weight 3, and FARGATE_SPOT with base 3 and weight 1
explanation: The base value sets how many tasks run on a provider first, so FARGATE with base 4 keeps the four required tasks on regular capacity. The weights then split extra tasks in a 1:3 ratio, placing about three of every four on Fargate Spot. Putting the base on Fargate Spot would risk interruptions for the minimum tasks. Only one provider in a strategy can have a base, and the other combinations give the wrong ratio.

question: A company wants to run a containerized machine learning inference service on Amazon ECS. The containers need NVIDIA GPUs and a specific instance type. Which configuration should a solutions architect choose?
options: Use the Fargate launch type and request NVIDIA GPUs with the resourceRequirements parameter in the task definition
Use Fargate Spot capacity providers so that GPU-enabled capacity is assigned to the tasks automatically
Use AWS App Runner with the largest available instance size of 4 vCPUs and 12 GB of memory
Use the EC2 launch type with GPU-based instances registered to the cluster through a capacity provider
explanation: GPU workloads on ECS run on EC2 container instances with GPUs, which also lets the company choose the exact instance type. Fargate does not offer GPUs or a choice of instance type, and Fargate Spot is the same platform at a lower price. App Runner does not provide GPU instances.

question: An Amazon ECS cluster uses the EC2 launch type. Service auto scaling adds tasks during peaks, but new tasks often stay in the PROVISIONING state because there are not enough container instances, and engineers add instances by hand. Which solution fixes this with the LEAST operational overhead?
options: Use an Auto Scaling group capacity provider with managed scaling enabled for the cluster
Add a scheduled scaling action to the Auto Scaling group that doubles capacity during business hours
Configure target tracking on the Auto Scaling group based on the average network traffic of the instances
Increase the task CPU and memory reservations so that fewer tasks are needed
explanation: With managed scaling, ECS calculates the capacity that pending and running tasks need and scales the Auto Scaling group to match, so new tasks get placed automatically. Scheduled scaling cannot react to unplanned demand. Network-based target tracking does not reflect unplaced tasks. Larger task reservations make placement harder, not easier.

question: An Amazon ECS service on AWS Fargate sits behind an Application Load Balancer. Load testing shows that each task handles about 500 requests per minute before latency rises, and CPU usage is not a good signal of load. How should the service scale?
options: Configure target tracking on the service's average CPU utilization at 70% so that tasks are added before saturation
Configure target tracking on the ALBRequestCountPerTarget metric with a target of about 500
Configure scheduled scaling actions that add tasks every morning at 08:00 and remove them at night
Configure the ALB to use the least outstanding requests algorithm so that busy tasks receive fewer requests
explanation: Target tracking on ALB requests per target keeps each task near the request rate it can handle, adding or removing tasks as traffic changes. CPU is known to be a poor signal for this service. Scheduled scaling does not follow real traffic. The load balancer distributes requests but does not change the number of tasks.

question: A company runs a payments container and a reporting container on the same Amazon ECS cluster. The security team requires that only the payments tasks can reach the payments database, even if both kinds of tasks run on the same host. Which configuration meets this requirement?
options: Use bridge network mode and allow the container instance security group as the source in the database security group
Use host network mode for better network performance and filter traffic with iptables rules inside each container
Use a network ACL on the database subnet that allows only the payments container's port from the cluster subnets
Use awsvpc network mode and assign a dedicated security group to the payments tasks that the database security group allows
explanation: In awsvpc mode, each task has its own elastic network interface and security groups, so the database can allow only the payments tasks' security group. In bridge or host mode, containers share the instance's network interface, so allowing the instance security group lets every container on it reach the database. Custom iptables rules are fragile. Network ACLs work on subnets and cannot tell tasks on the same host apart.

question: Amazon ECS tasks on AWS Fargate run in private subnets that have no route to the internet. The tasks must pull images from a private Amazon ECR repository and send logs to Amazon CloudWatch Logs. Which VPC endpoints are required? (Select THREE.)
options: A gateway VPC endpoint for Amazon S3, where ECR stores image layers
Interface VPC endpoints for the ECR API (ecr.api) and the Docker registry (ecr.dkr)
A gateway VPC endpoint for Amazon ECR in the private route tables
An interface VPC endpoint for Amazon EC2 so that Fargate can launch hosts
An interface VPC endpoint for CloudWatch Logs
An internet gateway with public IP addresses assigned to the tasks
explanation: Pulling from ECR privately needs the ecr.api and ecr.dkr interface endpoints plus access to S3, where image layers are stored, through a gateway endpoint. The awslogs driver needs a CloudWatch Logs endpoint. Gateway endpoints exist only for S3 and DynamoDB, not ECR. Fargate does not need an EC2 endpoint from the customer VPC. An internet gateway with public IPs would break the private-subnet design.

question: A content management system runs as Amazon ECS tasks on AWS Fargate across three Availability Zones. All tasks must read and write the same uploaded files, and the files must remain available when tasks are replaced. Which storage option should a solutions architect use?
options: An Amazon EFS file system mounted as a volume in the task definition
The ephemeral storage of each Fargate task increased to the maximum size
An Amazon EBS volume attached to one task and shared with the others over NFS
A bind mount to a host directory on the Fargate host
explanation: Amazon EFS is a Regional, multi-AZ file system that Fargate tasks can mount at the same time, and data persists when tasks are replaced. Fargate ephemeral storage belongs to a single task and is deleted when it stops. Sharing an EBS volume through one task creates a single point of failure. Bind mounts on Fargate use task storage, not durable shared storage.

question: During an Amazon ECS rolling deployment, a bad image caused new tasks to fail health checks repeatedly, and the service kept trying to start them for hours while capacity dropped. The company wants failed deployments to be detected and the previous working version restored automatically. What should a solutions architect configure?
options: Set the service's minimum healthy percent to 0 and maximum percent to 100
Enable the ECS deployment circuit breaker with rollback on the service
Increase the health check grace period of the service to several hours
Enable ECS managed instance draining on the cluster's capacity provider
explanation: The deployment circuit breaker marks a deployment as failed when tasks cannot reach a steady state, and with rollback enabled it returns the service to the last completed deployment. A minimum healthy percent of 0 allows all old tasks to stop, which makes things worse. A very long grace period only hides failing health checks. Managed draining handles EC2 instance terminations and is not related to deployments.

question: A team is new to Kubernetes. Which statement correctly describes a pod?
options: A pod is a group of worker nodes that share an Auto Scaling group and a launch template and are managed as one unit
A pod is the smallest deployable unit: one or more containers that share networking and storage and are scheduled together on a node
A pod is the control plane component that stores cluster state in etcd and schedules workloads onto the worker nodes
A pod is a load balancer that exposes a set of containers to traffic from outside the cluster through a stable IP address
explanation: In Kubernetes, a pod wraps one or more tightly coupled containers that share an IP address and volumes and always run on the same node. Groups of worker nodes are node groups. Cluster state is stored in etcd and scheduling is done by the scheduler in the control plane. External access is provided by Services and Ingress resources.

question: A company runs its applications on a self-managed Kubernetes cluster on premises and uses Helm charts and kubectl. It wants to move to AWS without rewriting manifests and without running the Kubernetes control plane itself. The control plane must be highly available. Which service should the company use?
options: Amazon EKS
Amazon ECS
AWS App Runner
AWS Elastic Beanstalk
explanation: Amazon EKS runs a managed, upstream-compatible Kubernetes control plane across multiple Availability Zones, so existing manifests, Helm charts, and kubectl keep working. ECS uses its own APIs and task definitions, so the workloads would need to be redefined. App Runner and Elastic Beanstalk are higher-level platforms that do not run Kubernetes workloads.

question: A company runs Amazon EKS with self-managed worker nodes. Upgrading node AMIs requires custom scripts to cordon, drain, and replace each node, and mistakes have caused outages. The company wants AWS to automate node provisioning and graceful updates while still using EC2 instances it can choose. Which option meets these requirements?
options: Migrate the workloads to EKS managed node groups
Migrate the workloads to an Amazon ECS cluster with the EC2 launch type
Keep self-managed nodes and add more nodes so that upgrades have spare capacity
Use EKS Distro on the existing EC2 instances
explanation: Managed node groups create and manage the EC2 instances and Auto Scaling group for the cluster and drain nodes gracefully during updates, while the company still picks instance types. Moving to ECS means replacing the Kubernetes workloads. Adding nodes does not automate upgrades. EKS Distro is a Kubernetes distribution for self-managed clusters and adds no node management.

question: A company runs a few small, bursty Kubernetes batch workloads on Amazon EKS. The worker nodes are mostly idle between bursts, and the team does not want to manage or right-size nodes for these workloads. Which solution will reduce cost and operational effort?
options: Create a larger managed node group and enable detailed monitoring on the instances to track the bursts more closely
Move the workloads to a self-managed node group on Dedicated Hosts so that the team controls instance placement
Run the workloads in Amazon EKS Anywhere on the company's existing on-premises servers to avoid EC2 charges
Create an EKS Fargate profile that selects the namespace of these workloads so that each pod runs on Fargate
explanation: With a Fargate profile, pods that match the selected namespace and labels run on right-sized Fargate capacity billed per pod, so there are no idle nodes to manage or pay for. A larger node group raises cost. Dedicated Hosts are the most expensive option and still need management. EKS Anywhere moves the work to company hardware and does not remove node management.

question: A company runs all of its Amazon EKS pods on AWS Fargate. The team now needs to deploy a monitoring agent as a Kubernetes DaemonSet so that one copy runs on every node, but the agent pods are never scheduled. Which solution meets this requirement?
options: Increase the vCPU and memory in the Fargate profile so that the DaemonSet pods have enough capacity to be scheduled
Add an EKS managed node group for the DaemonSet, or run the agent as a sidecar container in the Fargate pods
Add the DaemonSet's namespace and labels to the Fargate profile selectors so that the agent pods match the profile
Enable privileged mode on the Fargate pods that run the DaemonSet so that the agent can access the host
explanation: Each Fargate pod runs on its own dedicated compute and Fargate does not support DaemonSets, so the agent must run on EC2 nodes or be added as a sidecar to the application pods. Fargate profiles do not change this limit. Fargate also does not support privileged containers.

question: Several applications run as pods on the same Amazon EKS managed node group. One application must read objects from an Amazon S3 bucket, and the others must not have that access. Which solution follows the principle of least privilege?
options: Add the S3 permissions to the managed node group's IAM role, which the pods obtain through the instance metadata service
Store an IAM user's access keys in a Kubernetes Secret that is mounted by every pod in the namespace
Associate an IAM role with the application's Kubernetes service account by using EKS Pod Identity or IAM roles for service accounts
Add the S3 permissions to the EKS cluster IAM role that the control plane uses to manage AWS resources
explanation: EKS Pod Identity and IAM roles for service accounts give temporary credentials to pods that use a specific service account, so only that application gets S3 access. The node role is available to every pod on the node. Long-term keys in a Secret are insecure and shared. The cluster role is used by the control plane, not by application pods.

question: A manufacturer must keep some containerized workloads on servers in its factories because of data residency rules, but it wants to manage them with the same Amazon ECS APIs and console it uses in AWS. Which steps are required to use Amazon ECS Anywhere? (Select TWO.)
options: Deploy an AWS Outposts rack in each factory before registering the servers so that ECS can schedule tasks locally
Install the AWS Systems Manager Agent and the ECS agent on the factory servers by using an SSM activation to register them as external instances
Migrate the containers to the Fargate launch type so that they can run on the factory servers as external capacity
Make sure the factory servers have outbound connectivity to the AWS service endpoints
Create an Amazon EKS Fargate profile that targets the factory servers
explanation: ECS Anywhere registers on-premises servers as external instances through an SSM activation, and the SSM and ECS agents need outbound connectivity to AWS to receive tasks. Outposts is a different service and is not required. Fargate runs only in AWS Regions. EKS Fargate profiles belong to EKS, not ECS.

question: A telecom company must run Kubernetes clusters in its own data centers on VMware vSphere and bare metal. It wants AWS-supported tooling to create and upgrade the clusters, the same Kubernetes distribution that Amazon EKS uses, and the option to buy AWS support. Which option meets these requirements?
options: Amazon EKS Distro used alone
Amazon ECS Anywhere
Amazon EKS with managed node groups
Amazon EKS Anywhere
explanation: EKS Anywhere provides tooling to create and manage Kubernetes clusters on customer infrastructure, is based on EKS Distro, and offers an optional paid support subscription. EKS Distro on its own is just the open-source Kubernetes distribution, and the customer handles all cluster tooling and support. ECS Anywhere runs ECS tasks, not Kubernetes. Managed node groups run only in AWS Regions.

question: A small team that is new to AWS has a containerized web application in Amazon ECR. The team wants to provide only the image and IAM roles and have AWS provision the load balancer with HTTPS, automatic scaling, monitoring, and networking, without designing clusters, target groups, or load balancers itself. Which option should the team use?
options: Amazon ECS Express Mode
Amazon ECS on the EC2 launch type
Amazon EKS with a Fargate profile
AWS Batch with a Fargate compute environment
explanation: An Amazon ECS Express Mode service needs only a container image, a task execution role, and an infrastructure role, and it provisions a Fargate service with a URL, a load balancer with TLS, auto scaling, monitoring, and networking. AWS App Runner offered a similar experience but is no longer open to new customers, and AWS recommends ECS Express Mode instead. ECS on EC2 requires clusters, instances, and load balancers. EKS needs Kubernetes knowledge and setup. AWS Batch is for batch jobs, not web services.

question: A company is moving a chat server that keeps thousands of long-lived TCP connections open and runs continuously. It is packaged as a container image and needs 4 vCPUs and 8 GB of memory per copy. The company wants to avoid managing servers. Which compute option is the MOST suitable?
options: AWS Lambda functions invoked through a function URL
Amazon ECS on AWS Fargate behind a Network Load Balancer
AWS Batch jobs submitted every 15 minutes
AWS Lambda functions packaged as container images
explanation: Fargate runs long-lived containers without server management, and a Network Load Balancer supports long-lived TCP connections. Lambda invocations end after at most 15 minutes and are not built to hold persistent connections, whether packaged as .zip files or container images. Batch is meant for jobs that finish, not continuously running servers.

question: A company runs a steady baseline of Amazon ECS tasks on AWS Fargate and many AWS Lambda functions, and it plans to move some workloads to Amazon EC2 next year. The company wants a commitment-based discount that covers all of these services. Which purchase option should a solutions architect recommend?
options: EC2 Instance Savings Plans
Standard Reserved Instances
Compute Savings Plans
Fargate Spot capacity reservations
explanation: Compute Savings Plans apply to EC2, Fargate, and Lambda usage, whatever the instance family or Region, so they cover the current and future mix. EC2 Instance Savings Plans and Reserved Instances apply only to EC2. Fargate Spot is discounted spare capacity and cannot be reserved or committed to.

question: A company resizes images uploaded to Amazon S3. Uploads happen a few hundred times a day at random times, and each resize takes about 3 seconds. Today a container runs all day on AWS Fargate and polls for new files. Which change will be the MOST cost-effective?
options: Move the container to Fargate Spot and keep polling the bucket
Move the container to an Amazon EKS cluster with a managed node group
Move the container to a larger Fargate task size so that it polls more often
Use an AWS Lambda function triggered by S3 event notifications to resize each image
explanation: Lambda runs only when an upload event arrives and bills per millisecond, so a few hundred short jobs a day cost much less than an always-on container. Fargate Spot lowers the price but still pays for idle polling. EKS adds a cluster fee and nodes. A larger task increases idle cost.

question: An Amazon ECS service on AWS Fargate needs a database password at startup. Developers currently put the password in plaintext in the task definition environment variables. Which solution keeps the password out of the task definition with the LEAST code change?
options: Store the password in AWS Secrets Manager and reference it in the secrets section of the container definition
Store the password in the container image as a file so that it is not visible in the task definition or the console
Store the password in an encrypted Amazon S3 object and download it in the container entrypoint script at startup
Store the password in an Amazon EFS file that is mounted by all tasks of the service with encryption at rest
explanation: The secrets section of a container definition references a Secrets Manager secret or Systems Manager Parameter Store parameter, and ECS injects the value as an environment variable at startup, so the application code does not change. Putting the password in the image exposes it to anyone who can pull the image. Downloading from S3 needs script changes and extra protection. A shared file on EFS is harder to protect and rotate.

question: A company runs stateless, fault-tolerant web workloads on Amazon EKS using managed node groups of On-Demand x86 instances. The container images are already built for both x86 and arm64. The company wants to lower compute costs without changing application code. Which actions should a solutions architect recommend? (Select TWO.)
options: Use AWS Graviton-based instance types for the nodes that run the arm64 images
Move all pods to larger On-Demand instance types to reduce the number of nodes
Add managed node groups or Karpenter node pools that use EC2 Spot Instances across several instance types
Switch the node root volumes to Provisioned IOPS SSD (io2) volumes
Run every pod on EKS Fargate with the largest pod size available
explanation: Spot Instances spread across several instance types give large savings for interruption-tolerant workloads, and Graviton instances offer better price-performance for images that already support arm64. Larger On-Demand instances do not lower the hourly rate. io2 volumes cost more than gp3. Oversized Fargate pods pay for unused capacity.

question: An Amazon ECS service uses the EC2 launch type on an Auto Scaling group that spans three Availability Zones. To save money, an engineer set the service's task placement strategy to binpack on memory only. After an Availability Zone outage, the team discovered that all 12 tasks had been packed onto instances in a single Availability Zone. The company wants tasks balanced across Availability Zones while still using as few instances as possible within each zone. Which placement strategy should the service use?
options: binpack on memory followed by spread on instanceId
random placement with a distinctInstance placement constraint
spread on attribute:ecs.availability-zone followed by binpack on memory
spread on instanceId followed by spread on attribute:ecs.availability-zone
explanation: Strategies are applied in the order listed, so spreading on the Availability Zone attribute first balances tasks across zones, and binpack on memory then fills each instance before using another one in that zone. Binpack first would still concentrate tasks wherever capacity is free. Random placement with distinctInstance puts one task per instance, which increases the instance count and does not guarantee zone balance. Spreading by instance first spreads tasks over as many instances as possible, which works against the cost goal.

question: An Amazon ECS cluster that uses the EC2 launch type contains a mix of general purpose and compute optimized container instances. A CPU-heavy pricing engine must run only on the compute optimized c7i instances, while other services may run anywhere. How should a solutions architect make sure the pricing engine tasks are placed correctly?
options: Add a memberOf task placement constraint with an expression that matches attribute:ecs.instance-type =~ c7i.*
Add a binpack placement strategy on CPU so that the scheduler prefers the largest instances
Add a distinctInstance placement constraint so that each task gets a dedicated instance
Set the task definition CPU value higher than the vCPU count of the general purpose instances
explanation: A memberOf constraint uses the cluster query language to limit placement to container instances that match an expression, and ecs.instance-type is a built-in attribute, so the tasks land only on c7i instances. Placement strategies are best effort and do not restrict where tasks can run. distinctInstance places each task on a different instance but does not choose the instance type. Oversizing the CPU reservation is an indirect trick that wastes capacity and breaks when instance sizes change.

question: A company runs a customer-facing Amazon ECS service behind an Application Load Balancer. For each release, the team wants to start the new version next to the current one, send test traffic to it through a separate test listener, shift production traffic only after validation, and keep the old version running for a bake period so that it can switch back instantly if problems appear. Which deployment approach meets these requirements?
options: A rolling update with minimum healthy percent set to 50 and maximum percent set to 100
A rolling update with the deployment circuit breaker enabled
Deleting the service and recreating it with the new task definition during a maintenance window
An Amazon ECS blue/green deployment that uses a test listener, lifecycle hooks, and a bake time
explanation: ECS blue/green deployments run the blue and green service revisions side by side, can route test traffic to the green revision before production traffic shifts, and keep the blue revision during the bake time so that a rollback is quick. A rolling update replaces tasks gradually and cannot validate the new version with test traffic first. The circuit breaker rolls back only when tasks fail to reach a steady state. Recreating the service causes downtime.

question: An Amazon ECS service on AWS Fargate runs 6 tasks. During rolling deployments, the service temporarily drops to 3 healthy tasks and customers see slow responses. The company wants deployments to never reduce the number of healthy tasks below 6. Which deployment configuration should be used?
options: Minimum healthy percent 50 and maximum percent 100
Minimum healthy percent 100 and maximum percent 200
Minimum healthy percent 0 and maximum percent 200
Minimum healthy percent 100 and maximum percent 100
explanation: A minimum healthy percent of 100 keeps all 6 tasks running and healthy, and a maximum percent of 200 lets ECS start up to 6 new tasks before it stops old ones. A minimum of 50 or 0 allows ECS to stop old tasks first, which causes the capacity drop. With both values at 100, ECS can neither start nor stop a task, so the deployment cannot make progress.

question: An Amazon ECS service behind an Application Load Balancer uses rolling deployments with the deployment circuit breaker enabled. A recent release started and passed health checks normally, but a bug made the application return HTTP 500 errors for many requests. The circuit breaker did not roll back the deployment. How can the company make ECS roll back automatically in this situation?
options: Configure CloudWatch alarms on the load balancer's 5XX error metrics in the service's deployment configuration with rollback enabled
Lower the ALB health check interval and unhealthy threshold so that the circuit breaker detects the failing tasks faster
Enable task scale-in protection on the service so that tasks from the previous revision are kept running for rollback
Switch the service to the Fargate Spot capacity provider so that unhealthy tasks are replaced more often during deployments
explanation: The circuit breaker fails a deployment when tasks cannot start or reach a steady state, while deployment alarms fail it when a chosen CloudWatch alarm, such as one on ALB 5XX errors, enters the ALARM state, and both can roll back to the last completed deployment. A faster health check does not help if the health check path still succeeds. Scale-in protection keeps tasks from being stopped but does not detect failures or roll back. Fargate Spot changes the pricing model, not deployment safety.

question: A company is splitting an application into 15 Amazon ECS services on AWS Fargate. The services call each other over HTTP. The team wants each service to reach the others by short names such as http://orders:8080, with load balancing across tasks, retries of failed connections to unhealthy tasks, and consistent traffic metrics, without deploying an internal load balancer for every service. Which solution meets these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?
options: Create an internal Application Load Balancer for each service and store the DNS names in Parameter Store
Run an NGINX reverse proxy service that the other services call for every request
Configure Amazon ECS Service Connect with a shared AWS Cloud Map namespace for the services
Assign Elastic IP addresses to each task and publish them in a Route 53 private hosted zone
explanation: Service Connect adds a managed proxy to each task, so services call each other by short names within a Cloud Map namespace, with round-robin load balancing, outlier detection, and standard metrics in the ECS and CloudWatch consoles. One internal ALB per service adds cost and configuration. A self-managed NGINX tier is another component to scale and maintain. Fargate tasks in private subnets do not use Elastic IP addresses, and static records would break when tasks are replaced.

question: Engineers occasionally need a shell inside running Amazon ECS containers on AWS Fargate to troubleshoot production issues. The security team does not allow SSH keys, bastion hosts, or inbound ports, and every command that is run must be logged. Which solution meets these requirements?
options: Install an SSH server in the container image and allow port 22 from the corporate IP range
Enable ECS Exec on the service and send session logs to Amazon CloudWatch Logs or Amazon S3
Turn on VPC Flow Logs and use them to reconstruct the commands that engineers run
Run a bastion host in a public subnet and connect to the task's private IP address
explanation: ECS Exec uses AWS Systems Manager Session Manager to open a shell or run commands in a container on Fargate or EC2 without inbound ports or SSH keys, records who connected through the ExecuteCommand event in CloudTrail, and can log commands and output to CloudWatch Logs or S3. An SSH server and a bastion host both break the rules the security team set. Flow Logs record network metadata, not commands.

question: A genomics team runs a containerized job on Amazon ECS with AWS Fargate. Each task downloads about 120 GB of reference files, processes them, and discards everything when the task ends. Tasks currently fail with 'no space left on device'. Which change fixes the problem with the LEAST effort?
options: Move the job to the EC2 launch type and attach a larger root volume to each instance
Mount an Amazon S3 bucket as the container's root file system
Increase the task memory so that the files can be held in RAM
Set the ephemeralStorage parameter in the task definition to about 150 GiB
explanation: Fargate tasks get 20 GiB of ephemeral storage by default, and the ephemeralStorage parameter can raise it up to 200 GiB, which fits temporary scratch data that does not need to persist. Moving to EC2 adds instance management. S3 cannot be used as a container root file system. Holding 120 GB in memory is far more expensive and may exceed Fargate task sizes.

question: A company runs a transaction-heavy containerized database cache as an Amazon ECS service on AWS Fargate. Each task needs its own high-IOPS block storage volume, preloaded from a nightly snapshot, and the data does not need to be shared with other tasks or kept after a task stops. Which storage option meets these requirements?
options: Configure an Amazon EBS volume for each task at deployment time, created from the snapshot
Mount one Amazon EFS file system in all tasks and copy the snapshot data into it
Use Fargate ephemeral storage and download the data from Amazon S3 in the container entrypoint
Attach one existing Amazon EBS volume to all tasks in the service
explanation: ECS can attach one new Amazon EBS volume per task, including on Fargate, and the volume can be created from a snapshot, giving each task dedicated block storage for transaction-intensive workloads; volumes for service tasks are deleted when the task ends. EFS is shared file storage, not dedicated block storage per task. Downloading data at every start adds delay and custom code. ECS cannot attach an existing EBS volume, and one volume cannot be shared by all tasks.
subtopic: Amazon EBS volumes for ECS tasks

question: An Amazon ECS service processes video transcoding jobs from an Amazon SQS queue, and some jobs run for up to 3 hours. When service auto scaling scales in during quiet periods, it sometimes stops tasks in the middle of a job, and the work must start over. What should a solutions architect do?
options: Set the service minimum healthy percent to 100 so that running tasks are never stopped while the service changes size
Increase the SQS visibility timeout to 12 hours, the maximum, so that interrupted jobs are not lost or processed twice
Have each task set task scale-in protection through the ECS agent endpoint when it starts a job and clear it when the job finishes
Disable service auto scaling and run the maximum number of tasks at all times so that no task is ever scaled in
explanation: Task scale-in protection stops service auto scaling and deployments from terminating a protected task, and a task can set and clear the protection itself through the container agent endpoint around each job. Minimum healthy percent applies to deployments, not to scale-in. A longer visibility timeout only delays the retry of a job that was already interrupted. Running the maximum number of tasks all the time wastes money.

question: An Amazon ECS cluster runs many small tasks in awsvpc network mode on c5.large container instances. Each instance has plenty of spare CPU and memory, but only two tasks can be placed on it, so the cluster keeps adding instances. Which change will let the company run more tasks per instance and reduce the number of instances?
options: Switch the tasks to host network mode so that they share the instance network interface
Assign a secondary private IP address to each instance for every additional task
Increase the CPU and memory reservations in the task definition
Turn on the awsvpcTrunking account setting and launch new supported container instances
explanation: Each awsvpc task needs its own ENI, and a c5.large supports only a few ENIs; with ENI trunking turned on, newly launched supported instances get a trunk interface and can host many more awsvpc tasks, such as ten instead of two on a c5.large. Host mode removes per-task security groups and causes port conflicts. Secondary IP addresses do not give tasks their own ENIs. Larger reservations reduce density further.

question: A company runs a Linux-based Go API on Amazon ECS with AWS Fargate. The container image is already built for both x86 and arm64. The company wants to lower its Fargate compute bill without changing the application or managing servers. What should a solutions architect recommend?
options: Move the tasks to the EC2 launch type with x86 On-Demand Instances, which have no per-task Fargate charge
Set the task definition runtime platform CPU architecture to ARM64 so that the tasks run on AWS Graviton
Double the task CPU so that requests finish faster and fewer tasks are needed to handle the same load
Move the tasks to Windows containers on Fargate and reduce the task size to the smallest supported configuration
explanation: Fargate supports 64-bit ARM Linux tasks on AWS Graviton, and the published per-vCPU and per-GB rates for Linux/ARM are lower than for Linux/x86, so an image that already supports arm64 saves money with no code change. The EC2 launch type adds server management. Doubling CPU raises the price per second. Windows containers do not lower the cost and would require rebuilding the application.

question: A company keeps an Amazon ECS service with one Fargate task running all day, but the task only does useful work for 10 minutes at 01:00 every night when it exports reports. Which change will reduce costs the MOST while keeping the container image unchanged?
options: Run the container as a standalone ECS task started by an Amazon EventBridge Scheduler cron schedule
Keep the service and reduce the task size to the smallest Fargate configuration of 0.25 vCPU and 0.5 GB of memory
Move the service to a small EC2 instance that runs all day and start the export with a cron job
Keep the service and buy a Compute Savings Plan, which also applies to Fargate usage, for the task
explanation: EventBridge Scheduler can call the ECS RunTask API on a cron schedule, so the task runs only for the nightly export and Fargate charges only for those minutes. A smaller task or a Savings Plan still pays for 24 hours of idle time. An always-on EC2 instance adds management and still pays for idle hours.

question: An Amazon ECS service on AWS Fargate reads orders from an Amazon SQS queue. Each task can process about 50 messages per minute, and queue depth swings from almost zero to 40,000 messages within minutes. CPU utilization is a poor signal of load. How should the service scale so that the backlog per task stays near a chosen value?
options: Use target tracking on the service's average CPU utilization at 60% so that tasks are added as processing work increases
Use scheduled scaling that doubles the task count during business hours, when most orders arrive in the queue
Use step scaling on the queue's NumberOfMessagesSent metric with larger steps as more messages arrive
Use target tracking with a metric math expression that divides ApproximateNumberOfMessagesVisible by the service's RunningTaskCount
explanation: Application Auto Scaling target tracking can use a metric math expression, and dividing visible messages by running tasks gives backlog per task, so the service adds or removes tasks to keep each task's backlog near the target. CPU does not reflect queue depth here. Scheduled scaling ignores real load. NumberOfMessagesSent measures how fast messages arrive, not how much work is waiting for each task.

question: A company runs Amazon ECS tasks on AWS Fargate. The logging team wants container stdout logs sent to Amazon Data Firehose for delivery to Amazon S3 and also to an AWS Partner observability platform, with filtering applied before the logs leave the task. Developers do not want to change application code. Which solution meets these requirements?
options: Use the awslogs log driver and create CloudWatch Logs subscription filters for each destination
Configure FireLens in the task definition with an AWS for Fluent Bit log router container
Install the CloudWatch agent on the Fargate hosts and configure multiple outputs
Have each application write logs directly to Amazon S3 with the AWS SDK
explanation: FireLens adds a Fluent Bit or Fluentd log router to the task through task definition parameters, so stdout logs can be filtered and routed to Firehose and to partner destinations without code changes. Subscription filters work after logs reach CloudWatch Logs, which adds a hop and cost. Fargate gives no access to hosts for installing agents. Writing logs with the SDK requires code changes.

question: A batch-processing service runs on Amazon ECS with Fargate Spot capacity. When AWS reclaims capacity, some tasks stop before they save their progress to Amazon S3, and work is lost. The team wants each task to use the full warning period to checkpoint its work. Which actions should a solutions architect recommend? (Select TWO.)
options: Update the application to catch the SIGTERM signal and write a checkpoint when it is received
Configure Fargate to fall back to regular Fargate capacity automatically when Spot capacity is reclaimed
Turn on termination protection for the Fargate Spot tasks
Set the container stopTimeout to 120 seconds in the task definition
Increase the task size so that the work finishes before an interruption
explanation: Fargate Spot gives a two-minute warning through an EventBridge task state change event and a SIGTERM signal to the task, and the container is killed after stopTimeout, which defaults to 30 seconds and can be raised to 120 seconds. Catching SIGTERM and allowing 120 seconds lets the task save its work. Fargate does not replace Spot capacity with on-demand capacity on its own. No protection setting can stop a Spot interruption when AWS needs the capacity back. A larger task size does not prevent interruptions.

question: A company is starting a new Amazon EKS cluster. The small platform team does not want to install or maintain Karpenter, the load balancer controller, or the EBS CSI driver, and it wants AWS to choose, patch, and replace the worker nodes automatically while workloads keep using standard Kubernetes manifests. Which option meets these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?
options: EKS self-managed node groups with a custom AMI pipeline
EKS managed node groups with the Cluster Autoscaler installed
Amazon EKS Auto Mode
Amazon EKS Anywhere on EC2 instances
explanation: EKS Auto Mode has AWS manage the cluster infrastructure, including Karpenter-based compute autoscaling, node patching and replacement, load balancing integration, and EBS block storage, so these do not have to be installed as add-ons. Self-managed nodes need the most work. Managed node groups still leave the autoscaler and other add-ons to the team. EKS Anywhere is for running clusters on customer-managed infrastructure.

question: A retailer has servers in its stores that are connected to AWS through reliable AWS Direct Connect links. It wants to run Kubernetes workloads on these servers, but it does not want to operate a Kubernetes control plane on premises; the control plane should be managed by AWS and highly available. Which solution meets these requirements?
options: Amazon EKS Anywhere clusters installed on the store servers and connected to the EKS console with EKS Connector
Amazon EKS Hybrid Nodes that join the store servers to an Amazon EKS cluster in an AWS Region
Amazon ECS Anywhere with the store servers registered as external instances in a Regional cluster
Amazon EKS Distro installed on the store servers with kubeadm, using the same Kubernetes builds as EKS
explanation: EKS Hybrid Nodes let on-premises and edge machines join an EKS cluster whose control plane AWS manages in a Region, over a reliable connection such as Direct Connect or Site-to-Site VPN. EKS Anywhere and EKS Distro run the control plane on customer infrastructure; EKS Anywhere is the better fit only for disconnected environments. ECS Anywhere runs ECS tasks, not Kubernetes workloads.

question: An Amazon EKS cluster runs workloads with very different CPU, memory, and GPU needs. The team maintains eight node groups, one per instance type, and many nodes are only half used. The company wants nodes that are right-sized for pending pods, launched in under a minute, and removed or consolidated when they are no longer needed. Which solution meets these requirements?
options: Install Karpenter and define node pools that allow a broad set of instance types
Increase the minimum size of each node group so that pods never wait for capacity
Replace all node groups with one node group of the largest instance type
Use scheduled scaling on each node group's Auto Scaling group
explanation: Karpenter watches for unschedulable pods and launches right-sized EC2 instances that match their compute, storage, and accelerator needs, usually in under a minute, and it removes nodes that are no longer needed. Larger minimum sizes and one oversized instance type increase waste. Scheduled scaling does not respond to actual pod demand.

question: A web application on Amazon EKS managed node groups must handle traffic that triples during sales. The number of pods should grow with CPU load, and the cluster should add nodes when new pods cannot be scheduled. Which components should a solutions architect use? (Select TWO.)
options: A Kubernetes DaemonSet that runs one copy of the application on every node
The Horizontal Pod Autoscaler with the Kubernetes Metrics Server installed
An EKS Fargate profile for the kube-system namespace
AWS Global Accelerator in front of the cluster
Karpenter or the Kubernetes Cluster Autoscaler
explanation: The Horizontal Pod Autoscaler changes the number of pods based on CPU utilization and needs a metrics source such as the Metrics Server, while Karpenter or the Cluster Autoscaler adds nodes when pods cannot be scheduled. A DaemonSet runs one pod per node and does not follow load. A Fargate profile for kube-system does not scale the application. Global Accelerator improves network paths but does not add capacity.

question: A company needs to give a group of developers, who assume an IAM role, read-only kubectl access to one namespace of an Amazon EKS cluster. The platform team wants to manage this through the EKS API and infrastructure as code, with access changes logged in AWS CloudTrail, instead of editing a ConfigMap inside the cluster. What should the platform team do?
options: Add the developers' IAM role to the aws-auth ConfigMap in the kube-system namespace and map it to the system:masters group
Attach the AmazonEKSClusterPolicy managed policy to the developers' IAM role so that they can call the cluster
Create IAM users for each developer and share the cluster creator's credentials, which have admin access by default
Create an EKS access entry for the IAM role and associate a view access policy scoped to that namespace
explanation: EKS access entries map an IAM principal to Kubernetes permissions through the EKS API, and access policies, which can be scoped to namespaces, give predefined permissions such as view. The aws-auth ConfigMap is the legacy method, and system:masters would grant full admin rights. AmazonEKSClusterPolicy is for the cluster role, not for users. Sharing the creator's credentials breaks least privilege and auditing.

question: A financial company's security policy states that the Kubernetes API server of its Amazon EKS cluster must not be reachable from the internet. Administrators connect from the corporate network over AWS Direct Connect to the cluster's VPC. How should the cluster endpoint be configured?
options: Keep the public endpoint enabled and restrict the public access CIDRs to the corporate network's public IP range
Keep public access enabled and associate an AWS WAF web ACL with the endpoint that allows only the corporate network
Disable public endpoint access, enable private endpoint access, and allow the corporate network on port 443 in the cluster security group
Create a gateway VPC endpoint for Amazon EKS in the cluster VPC and remove the internet gateway from the VPC
explanation: With public access disabled and private access enabled, the API server can only be reached from within the VPC or a connected network, and the cluster security group controls access to the private endpoint. Limiting public CIDRs still leaves the endpoint on the internet. AWS WAF cannot be attached to the EKS API endpoint. Gateway endpoints exist only for S3 and DynamoDB.

question: A FinOps review finds that several Amazon EKS clusters cost more per cluster hour than others even though they have the same number of nodes. The expensive clusters run a Kubernetes minor version that was released on EKS more than 14 months ago. What is the MOST likely cause, and how can the company reduce the cost?
options: The clusters run more control plane instances because of their age; delete them and recreate them in another Region
The clusters are in extended support, which has an additional per-cluster-hour charge; upgrade them to a version in standard support
The clusters use EKS Pod Identity, which is billed for each pod association; switch to IAM roles for service accounts
The clusters use managed node groups, which add a per-node management fee; switch to self-managed node groups
explanation: An EKS Kubernetes version gets 14 months of standard support and then 12 months of extended support, which adds a charge per cluster hour; upgrading to a version in standard support removes that charge. The control plane is not billed per instance in this way. Pod Identity has no per-association fee. Managed node groups have no additional cost beyond the resources they use.

question: A content platform runs on Amazon EKS with nodes in three Availability Zones. Pods in all zones must read and write the same set of uploaded files at the same time, and pods that are rescheduled to another zone must still see the files. Which storage solution should a solutions architect choose?
options: Amazon EBS gp3 volumes provisioned dynamically through the EBS CSI driver for each pod
The node's local NVMe instance store mounted into the pods with a hostPath volume
An Amazon S3 bucket mounted into every pod as an emptyDir volume
An Amazon EFS file system mounted as a persistent volume through the EFS CSI driver
explanation: The EFS CSI driver lets pods mount an Amazon EFS file system as a persistent volume, and EFS is a Regional file system that many pods across Availability Zones can use at the same time. EBS volumes belong to one Availability Zone and are attached to a single node. Instance store data is lost when the node goes away. An emptyDir volume is temporary pod storage, not an S3 mount.

question: A healthcare company runs Amazon EKS clusters on a current Kubernetes version. An auditor requires that Kubernetes Secrets stored in etcd be encrypted with a key that the company controls, can disable, and whose use is recorded in AWS CloudTrail. What should a solutions architect do?
options: Nothing; the default envelope encryption already uses a customer managed key in the company's account
Enable EBS encryption by default for the account so that etcd volumes use a company key
Associate a customer managed AWS KMS key with the cluster for envelope encryption of Kubernetes API data
Store all secrets in a ConfigMap encrypted with a key that is kept in the container image
explanation: EKS envelope encrypts all Kubernetes API data by default, but with an AWS owned key; associating a customer managed KMS key gives the company control over the key and CloudTrail records of its use. The default key is not in the customer account. Account-level EBS encryption affects the company's own volumes, not the managed control plane's etcd. Keeping a key in an image is insecure.

question: A team moved a pod from an Amazon EKS managed node group to AWS Fargate by using a Fargate profile. The pod uses an EKS Pod Identity association to get an IAM role for Amazon DynamoDB, and since the move its AWS SDK calls fail because no credentials are found. How should the team give the Fargate pod IAM permissions?
options: Use IAM roles for service accounts by creating an IAM OIDC provider for the cluster and annotating the service account with the role
Run the EKS Pod Identity Agent as a DaemonSet on the Fargate nodes so that the association can deliver credentials
Attach the DynamoDB permissions to the Fargate pod execution role that is specified in the Fargate profile
Configure the AWS SDK in the pod to read credentials from the EC2 instance metadata service at 169.254.169.254
explanation: EKS Pod Identity is not supported for pods that run on Fargate, and the EKS documentation says to give Fargate pods IAM credentials through IAM roles for service accounts. DaemonSets do not run on Fargate. The pod execution role is used by Fargate infrastructure, for example to pull images, and is not meant for application permissions. IMDS is not available to Fargate pods.

question: A company runs an Amazon EKS cluster with a stateless image-rendering service that tolerates interruptions and a StatefulSet message broker that must not be interrupted. Both run on On-Demand managed node groups today. The company wants to cut compute cost while keeping both workloads available. Which actions should a solutions architect take? (Select TWO.)
options: Move the StatefulSet to a Spot managed node group with a single instance type to get the largest Spot discount
Run both workloads on one Spot managed node group that uses the largest available instance type so that fewer, bigger nodes are needed
Create a Spot managed node group that uses several instance types with the same vCPU and memory for the rendering pods
Run the rendering pods on EKS Fargate with Fargate Spot capacity to avoid managing nodes
Keep the StatefulSet on an On-Demand node group by scheduling it with the eks.amazonaws.com/capacityType: ON_DEMAND label
explanation: Spot managed node groups suit stateless, fault-tolerant work, and using several instance types with matching vCPU and memory widens the Spot capacity pools. Stateful, fault-intolerant workloads should stay on On-Demand nodes, which EKS labels with eks.amazonaws.com/capacityType so pods can target them. Putting the StatefulSet on Spot risks interruptions, and a single instance type reduces Spot availability. Amazon EKS does not support Fargate Spot.

question: A company builds container images in a central build account in us-east-1. For disaster recovery, every new image pushed to the production repositories must be copied automatically to Amazon ECR in a separate DR account in us-west-2. Which steps are required? (Select TWO.)
options: In the DR account, add a registry permissions policy that allows the build account to call ecr:ReplicateImage and ecr:CreateRepository
In the build account, add a repository policy on each source repository that allows the DR account to pull and replicate images
Schedule an AWS Lambda function that pulls each new image and pushes it to the repository in the DR account
In the build account's registry settings, create a replication rule with the DR account and us-west-2 as the destination
Enable S3 Cross-Region Replication on the Amazon S3 bucket that ECR uses to store the image layers
explanation: ECR cross-account replication is configured with replication rules in the source registry and a registry permissions policy in the destination account that allows the source account to replicate images and create repositories. Source repositories do not need special repository policies for replication. A Lambda copy job adds code to maintain. ECR manages its own storage, so customers cannot configure S3 replication on it.

question: A company wants to cache Docker Hub images in its Amazon ECR private registry to avoid anonymous pull limits. The security team requires that the Docker Hub access token never be stored in build scripts, task definitions, or node configuration. How should the pull through cache rule be set up?
options: Create the rule without credentials, because ECR authenticates to Docker Hub with its own service account
Store the token in an encrypted environment variable of every Amazon ECS task and EKS pod that pulls images through the cache
Store the token as a SecureString parameter in AWS Systems Manager Parameter Store and reference it from the repository policy
Store the Docker Hub credentials in an AWS Secrets Manager secret whose name starts with ecr-pullthroughcache/ and reference it in the rule
explanation: Docker Hub is an upstream registry that requires authentication for pull through cache, and ECR reads the credentials from a Secrets Manager secret with the ecr-pullthroughcache/ prefix in the same account and Region. Pull through cache for Docker Hub cannot be set up without credentials. Putting the token in tasks or pods spreads the secret everywhere. Repository policies cannot reference Parameter Store values.
subtopic: Amazon ECR pull through cache authentication

question: A company's Amazon ECR repository was created with the default encryption settings. A new compliance rule requires that the images be encrypted with a customer managed AWS KMS key that the company can audit and disable. What should a solutions architect do?
options: Edit the existing repository's encryption configuration to use the customer managed key, and ECR re-encrypts the stored images in place
Create a new repository with KMS encryption using the customer managed key, push the images to it, and update the image references
Enable default EBS encryption with the customer managed key in the account so that ECR uses that key for image layers
Turn on enhanced scanning so that images are re-encrypted with the customer managed key when they are rescanned
explanation: ECR encrypts images at rest with SSE-S3 by default and can use SSE-KMS with an AWS managed or customer managed key, but a repository's encryption configuration is set at creation and cannot be changed later, so a new repository is needed. EBS default encryption does not apply to ECR storage. Enhanced scanning finds vulnerabilities and does not change encryption.

question: An Amazon ECS service on AWS Fargate receives its database password as an environment variable from AWS Secrets Manager through the secrets section of the container definition. After Secrets Manager rotated the password, the running tasks started failing to connect to the database. What should the company do so that tasks use the new password after each rotation?
options: Nothing; ECS refreshes secrets from Secrets Manager inside running containers automatically after each rotation
Move the password into the container image so that it is always available, even when Secrets Manager rotates it
Start new tasks after rotation, for example by updating the service with the force new deployment option
Reduce the Secrets Manager rotation interval so that the value changes more often and tasks stay in sync
explanation: ECS injects secrets as environment variables only when the container starts, so a rotated value is picked up only by new tasks, which a forced new deployment of the service launches. Running containers are not updated automatically. Baking the password into the image exposes it and breaks rotation. Rotating more often makes the problem happen more often.

question: Two applications run as Amazon ECS services on AWS Fargate and share one Amazon EFS file system. Each application must be able to mount only its own directory, file access must be authorized with each service's task IAM role, and data must be encrypted in transit. Which configuration steps should a solutions architect take? (Select TWO.)
options: Place the two services in different subnets and use network ACLs to block each application from reaching the other application's directory
Create an EFS access point for each application with its own root directory and reference it in that application's task definition
Enable transit encryption and IAM authorization in the EFS volume configuration, and allow each task role to use only its own access point
Mount the file system root in both task definitions and set the container user to root so that file permissions are not an issue
Attach an Amazon S3 bucket policy that limits each task role to its own prefix in the shared file system
explanation: EFS access points enforce a root directory per application, and an ECS task definition can mount the file system through an access point with IAM authorization that uses the task role, which requires transit encryption to be enabled. Network ACLs cannot control access to directories. Mounting the root as root gives both applications full access. S3 bucket policies do not apply to EFS.

question: A software company runs untrusted, customer-supplied code in containers on Amazon ECS. The security team wants every task to run in its own isolated environment that does not share a kernel, network interface, ephemeral storage, CPU, or memory with other tasks. Which option meets this requirement with the LEAST operational overhead?
options: Run the tasks on the EC2 launch type with a distinctInstance placement constraint
Run the tasks on AWS Fargate
Run the tasks on the EC2 launch type in bridge network mode with separate Docker networks
Run all tasks on one large EC2 Dedicated Instance
explanation: Fargate runs each task in its own hardware virtualization environment, so tasks do not share network interfaces, ephemeral storage, CPU, or memory, and there are no instances to manage; AWS recommends Fargate for strong task isolation. distinctInstance is based on desired status and can briefly place two running tasks on one instance, and it still requires instance management. Bridge networks and a shared Dedicated Instance keep tasks on the same kernel.

question: An Amazon ECS cluster uses the EC2 launch type with an Auto Scaling group capacity provider. Average CPU and memory reservation across the instances is about 35%, and engineers adjust the instance count by hand. The company wants to run the same tasks on fewer instances automatically. Which actions should a solutions architect take? (Select TWO.)
options: Use the binpack placement strategy on memory for the services
Use the spread placement strategy on instanceId for the services
Turn on managed scaling for the capacity provider with a target capacity of 100%
Add a distinctInstance placement constraint to every service
Attach a scheduled scaling action that adds instances every hour
explanation: Binpack places tasks to leave the least unused CPU or memory, which minimizes the number of instances in use, and managed scaling with a target capacity of 100% lets ECS scale the Auto Scaling group in and out so that no idle spare instances are kept. Spreading by instance and distinctInstance spread tasks over more instances. Scheduled scale-out adds capacity regardless of need.
subtopic: ECS cluster auto scaling and binpack

question: A company plans to move all workloads in its Amazon EKS cluster from EC2 managed node groups to AWS Fargate. Which of the following workloads will need to stay on EC2 nodes? (Select THREE.)
options: A log collection agent deployed as a Kubernetes DaemonSet
A stateless REST API exposed through an Application Load Balancer with IP targets
A machine learning inference service that needs NVIDIA GPUs
A web application whose pods share an Amazon EFS file system
A database StatefulSet that stores its data on Amazon EBS volumes
A worker deployment scaled by the Horizontal Pod Autoscaler
explanation: EKS on Fargate does not support DaemonSets, GPUs, or mounting Amazon EBS volumes to pods, so those workloads must stay on EC2 nodes. Fargate pods can sit behind Application Load Balancers and Network Load Balancers with IP targets, can mount Amazon EFS file systems, and can be scaled by the Horizontal Pod Autoscaler.
